scene: A new student asks the surgical ward manager what this department is trying to achieve.
ask: What aim does the introduction give?

choices.text: Quality client-centered service, aiming at high efficiency, equity, and cost-effectiveness.
choices.note: Correct. The introduction says the Department of Surgery provides quality client-centered service, with an aim to achieve high efficiency, equity, and cost-effectiveness.

choices.text: High-technology surgery only, with equity left out of the aim.
choices.note: The same sentence keeps efficiency, equity, and cost-effectiveness together; it does not drop equity or reduce the aim to technology.

choices.text: Client-centered care that sets cost-effectiveness aside.
choices.note: Cost-effectiveness is named in the aim alongside efficiency and equity, not set aside.

choices.text: A manual whose only aim is to raise study pressure.
choices.note: Freedom from study pressure is the study-manual purpose on the next page, not this department-aim sentence.

scene: The theatre list marks a patient as HBP and the student checks the scope list.
ask: What specialty does this page attach to HBP?

choices.text: Head and Neck, written 頭頸外科.
choices.note: 頭頸外科 is the Chinese label for Head and Neck (H&N), not HBP.

choices.text: Liver Transplant, written 肝臟移植外科.
choices.note: 肝臟移植外科 belongs to Liver Transplant (LT), a separate scope item.

choices.text: Hepatobiliary and Pancreatic, written 肝膽胰外科.
choices.note: Correct. The scope line reads Hepatobiliary & Pancreatic (HBP: 肝膽胰外科).

choices.text: Ear, Nose and Throat, written 耳鼻喉外科.
choices.note: 耳鼻喉外科 is ENT, not the HBP line.

scene: Two gastrointestinal labels on the allocation sheet are easy to mix up.
ask: Which pairing does the note give for colorectal surgery?

choices.text: EGI, 消化道外科.
choices.note: EGI is Esophagus & Gastrointestinal, 消化道外科, not colorectal.

choices.text: CRS, 結腸直腸外科.
choices.note: Correct. The page prints Colorectal (CRS: 結腸直腸外科).

choices.text: SGEN, 普通外科.
choices.note: SGEN is General Surgery, 普通外科.

choices.text: BR, 乳房外科.
choices.note: BR is Breast, 乳房外科.

scene: The student is matching TSU and NS on the same scope list.
ask: What do those two codes stand for here?

choices.text: TSU is trauma surgery and NS is neck surgery.
choices.note: Trauma is not this code; Head and Neck is H&N, 頭頸外科, and NS is neurosurgery.

choices.text: TSU is transplant surgery and NS is nasal surgery.
choices.note: Liver Transplant is LT, and ear, nose and throat is ENT.

choices.text: Both codes sit under Plastic Surgery, PRS, 整形外科.
choices.note: PRS is its own scope item, separate from TSU and NS.

choices.text: TSU is Thoracic Surgery Unit, 胸外科, and NS is Neurosurgery, 神經外科.
choices.note: Correct. The page lists Thoracic Surgery Unit (TSU: 胸外科) and Neurosurgery (NS: 神經外科) as separate services.

scene: Endocrine is on the scope list but the Chinese label looks unfinished.
ask: What does the page actually print beside ECS?

choices.text: A completed Chinese label written in the same style as 泌尿外科.
choices.note: Urology has 泌尿外科; the ECS colon is empty in this extract.

choices.text: The same Chinese label as ENT, 耳鼻喉外科.
choices.note: ENT is a different item and does carry 耳鼻喉外科.

choices.text: Endocrine (ECS: ) with the Chinese label left blank.
choices.note: Correct. The line is Endocrine (ECS: ) while the neighbouring specialties have Chinese names filled in.

choices.text: ECS is omitted from the scope of services.
choices.note: Endocrine (ECS) is listed; only the Chinese wording is blank.

scene: The tutor says a surgical student may sometimes leave this ward for practicum, and asks why the manual exists.
ask: Which statement matches that introduction page?

choices.text: You may visit Orthopaedics and Traumatology (Trauma: 創傷及矯形外科), and the manual is so students can adapt, become a competence member, and keep studying without pressure from an unfamiliar environment.
choices.note: Correct. The page says sometimes you visit that department as a surgery clinical practicum location, and states that education-program purpose.

choices.text: Orthopaedics replaces every surgical specialty on the previous page.
choices.note: The page says sometimes you will visit it as a practicum location, not that it replaces the surgical scope.

choices.text: The purpose is to increase study pressure until the environment feels familiar.
choices.note: The note says continuous clinical study free from study pressure caused by an unfamiliar environment.

choices.text: Trauma is labelled 神經外科 and is the daily neurosurgical ward.
choices.note: 神經外科 is NS on the scope page; this page names 創傷及矯形外科.

scene: Before the first observation round, a student asks what vital signs are for.
ask: How does this vital-sign page describe them?

choices.text: Fixed adult numbers that do not change with age or condition.
choices.note: The page says normal ranges of measurements change with age and medical condition.

choices.text: A temperature-only check with no role in finding problems.
choices.note: The page ties vital signs to assessing basic functions and to detecting or monitoring medical problems.

choices.text: The same list as a septic workup, including cultures.
choices.note: Cultures are a later workup page; this page is about vital signs as basic measures.

choices.text: Measures of physiological status used to assess the most basic body functions, useful for detecting or monitoring medical problems, with normal ranges that change with age and medical condition.
choices.note: Correct. That is the page wording: measures of various physiological status, basic body functions, ranges that change with age and medical condition, and useful in detecting or monitoring medical problems.

scene: The tutor points at the examples of the body's most basic functions.
ask: Which measurements does that page list?

choices.text: Blood glucose and wound exudate only.
choices.note: Glucose and wound words are in later sections, not this list.

choices.text: Body temperature, blood pressure and pulse or heart rate, and oxygen saturation and respiration.
choices.note: Correct. The page lists body temperature (Temp), blood pressure (BP) and pulse / heart rate, and oxygen saturation and respiration.

choices.text: Temperature and blood pressure, leaving out oxygen saturation and respiration.
choices.note: Oxygen saturation and respiration are the third example group on the page.

choices.text: Pain score, PCA use, and drain output.
choices.note: Those appear in the return-to-ward notes, not in this vital-sign list.

scene: A tympanic reading looks lower than the patient feels, so you check the underestimate list.
ask: Which set does the note give as reasons for an underestimated tympanic temperature?

choices.text: The ear canal is not straightened and the probe is poorly inserted so air leaks, the ear is impacted with a lot of earwax, or the patient has just swallowed cold food or liquid.
choices.note: Correct. Those are the three underestimate factors cited from Timby, 2003.

choices.text: Hot food or drink, or lying with the ear covered.
choices.note: Those are the overestimate factors on the same page, not the underestimate list.

choices.text: A narrow blood-pressure cuff and talking during the reading.
choices.note: Cuff and talking problems are on the blood-pressure pages, not this tympanic list.

choices.text: Earwax only, after the canal was straightened and the probe sealed.
choices.note: Impacted earwax is one factor, but a canal that is not straightened with air leak, and cold food or liquid, are also listed.

scene: The next tympanic reading may be falsely high.
ask: What does the same page list as overestimate factors?

choices.text: Cold food and a lot of earwax.
choices.note: Cold intake and impacted earwax are underestimate factors.

choices.text: An unstraightened canal with an air leak around the probe.
choices.note: That probe and canal problem is listed under underestimate, not overestimate.

choices.text: The patient has just swallowed hot food or liquids, or has lain down and covered the ear.
choices.note: Correct. The overestimate factors are hot food or liquids, and lying down with the ear covered.

choices.text: Charting the higher of the two ears.
choices.note: Choosing the higher ear is a later low-temperature charting step, not an overestimate cause on this page.

scene: One ear reads 36.2 ℃ and the student asks whether that sits in the normal band printed for tympanic temperature.
ask: What normal range and what low-temperature cut-off does this page print?

choices.text: Normal 36.5℃ to 37.5℃, with low starting under 36.5℃.
choices.note: Those cut-offs are not printed; this page uses 36.0 ℃-37.6℃ and ≤35.9℃.

choices.text: Normal range 36.0 ℃-37.6℃, and low body temperature at ≤35.9℃.
choices.note: Correct. The low-temperature page prints normal range 36.0 ℃-37.6℃ and the action row ≤35.9℃ as low body temp.

choices.text: Normal 36.0 ℃-37.6℃, and 37.6℃ already counted as low body temperature.
choices.note: 37.6℃ is inside the printed normal top, and the low row is ≤35.9℃; the low-grade fever row starts on the next page.

choices.text: No range in this file, because vital signs are only a cross-reference to the medical FAQ.
choices.note: The section banner says vital signs are the same as the medical FAQ, but this page still prints 36.0 ℃-37.6℃ and ≤35.9℃.

scene: Recheck gives 35.4℃ in one ear and 36.1℃ in the other. The patient is not dizzy.
ask: What should you chart, and when do you tell the team nurse?

choices.text: Chart the lower ear so a low reading is not hidden, and phone the doctor yourself.
choices.note: The note says chart the higher result within or nearest normal, and the team nurse is the person who informs the doctor.

choices.text: Skip the recheck and apply Bair Hugger as the first step.
choices.note: Bair Hugger is the remark for when recheck and blankets still fail to keep a normal temperature.

choices.text: Report every ≤35.9℃ reading immediately, dizzy or not.
choices.note: Immediate report is for the dizziness case; otherwise the report is after routine.

choices.text: Recheck both ears at once, chart the higher result that is within or nearest the normal range, and report after the temperature routine.
choices.note: Correct. The action says recheck bilateral ears immediately, then chart the higher result which is within or nearest normal range, and report immediately only for a dizziness case; otherwise after routine.

scene: Both ears stay at or below 35.9℃ after the recheck, and the patient feels dizzy.
ask: Which still-low care matches the page?

choices.text: Ice pad, encourage fluid, and take blankets off.
choices.note: Ice, fluids, and removing blankets are the high-temperature care, not the low row.

choices.text: Blankets only, with no rail, no pulse or blood-pressure check, and no further temperature.
choices.note: If the patient is dizzy the page adds a bedside rail and a BP and pulse check, then a 15-30 minute recheck and a report.

choices.text: Add more blankets and keep bed rest; if dizzy, put up the bedside rail and check blood pressure and pulse; recheck the temperature after 15-30 minutes; tell the team nurse immediately because of dizziness.
choices.note: Correct. That is the numbered still-low care: blankets and bed rest, rail plus BP and pulse if dizzy, recheck after 15-30 minutes, and immediate report for dizziness. The team nurse informs the doctor.

choices.text: Raise the feet above the head before any blanket.
choices.note: Feet higher than the head is a low blood-pressure step, not this temperature list.

scene: Blankets and another temperature check still do not hold a normal reading.
ask: What may be used, and what is it?

choices.text: Bair Hugger, a temperature management system that uses forced warm air to prevent and treat hypothermia in surgical patients.
choices.note: Correct. The remark says if recheck and blankets still fail to keep a normal temperature, Bair Hugger may be applied, and the footnote defines it as forced warm air for hypothermia.

choices.text: An ice pad with a pillow cover, used as a warming hugger.
choices.note: Ice pads with a cover are on the high-temperature pages; this failure line names Bair Hugger.

choices.text: Nasal oxygen at 6 L/min as the hypothermia treatment.
choices.note: Those oxygen litres are on the saturation pages, not the low-temperature remark.

choices.text: Oral Panadol 500 mg started to warm the patient.
choices.note: Panadol 500 mg Q4H prn is the high-temperature example as a doctor's order, not this low-temperature line.

scene: After bilateral recheck the tympanic readings stay in the low-grade band. The patient is not dizzy and can drink.
ask: What care does the low-grade fever row describe?

choices.text: Phone the doctor at once and collect septic cultures yourself.
choices.note: On this band the team nurse informs the doctor during the ward round; a septic workup is the severe-fever remark.

choices.text: Chart whichever ear is further above normal, then add blankets.
choices.note: This page says chart the result within or nearest normal, and care includes removing extra blanket and clothing.

choices.text: Start Panadol 500 mg Q4H prn as a standing dose with no order.
choices.note: The page gives Panadol 500 mg Q4H prn as an example of administration as doctor order.

choices.text: The row is ≥37.6℃ and ≤38.5℃. Recheck both ears and chart the result within or nearest normal. If still high: ice pad with a cover, encourage water when there is no fluid restriction and no swallowing problem, remove extra blanket and clothing, recheck in 15-30 minutes, and give oral or per-rectal Panadol 500 mg Q4H prn only as the doctor orders.
choices.note: Correct. That is the low-grade action and nursing care. Report at once only for dizziness; otherwise after the temperature routine. The team nurse increases monitoring to Q4H and informs the doctor during the ward round.

scene: The temperature is still at or above 38.5℃ and the blood pressure looks low.
ask: How does the severe high-fever page differ from the low-grade row?

choices.text: Treat it exactly like low-grade fever and wait for the ward-round message.
choices.note: This page says the team nurse informs the doctor by phone immediately, and it adds blood pressure, pulse and SaO2.

choices.text: Call it high fever at ≥38.5℃. Recheck both ears; if still high, measure blood pressure, pulse and SaO2, and tell the team nurse at once if blood pressure or SaO2 is on the low side. If high temperature and low blood pressure remain, use the covered ice pad, water if allowed, removal of extra blankets and clothing, a 15-30 minute recheck, and doctor-ordered Panadol 500 mg Q4H prn. The team nurse phones the doctor immediately.
choices.note: Correct. Those are the severe-page actions and the phone-immediately remark. The doctor may order a septic workup, and temperature monitoring increases to Q4H.

choices.text: Do not recheck the ears once the first reading is ≥38.5℃.
choices.note: The action column still says recheck bilateral ears immediately.

choices.text: Start Bair Hugger because 38.5℃ is the hypothermia device threshold.
choices.note: Bair Hugger is the low-temperature forced-air remark, not this high-fever page.

scene: After a high fever the team nurse uses the words septic shock and asks what this page means.
ask: What definition is printed?

choices.text: A serious condition that occurs when a body-wide infection leads to dangerously low blood pressure.
choices.note: Correct. That is the opening definition on the septic-shock page.

choices.text: A local wound infection with a normal blood pressure.
choices.note: The page says a body-wide infection leading to dangerously low blood pressure.

choices.text: High blood pressure caused by toxins, without tissue damage.
choices.note: The page says toxins released by the bacteria or fungi may cause tissue damage, and defines the shock by low blood pressure.

choices.text: Only a mild fever that stays inside the low-grade band.
choices.note: Low-grade fever is the earlier temperature row; this page calls septic shock a serious condition.

scene: A student is listing who develops septic shock and what can cause it.
ask: Which account matches the page?

choices.text: Only middle-aged adults, and only one kind of bacteria.
choices.note: The page says most often the very old and the very young, and any type of bacteria.

choices.text: Viruses are the usual cause and bacteria are rare.
choices.note: Viruses may rarely cause it; any type of bacteria can cause it.

choices.text: It occurs most often in the very old and the very young, and may occur with a weakened immune system. Any type of bacteria can cause it. Fungi and, rarely, viruses may also cause it. Toxins may cause tissue damage.
choices.note: Correct. That matches the page: age groups, weakened immune systems, any bacteria, fungi, rarely viruses, and toxins causing tissue damage.

choices.text: Fungi are excluded, and toxins protect tissue.
choices.note: Fungi may cause it, and toxins may cause tissue damage.

scene: The tutor asks how the second septic-shock page links the illness to organs.
ask: What does that page say?

choices.text: Toxins raise blood pressure and improve organ function.
choices.note: The page says this may lead to low blood pressure and poor organ function.

choices.text: This may lead to low blood pressure and poor organ function. Some researchers think blood clots in small arteries cause the lack of blood flow and poor organ function. A strong inflammatory response to the toxins may contribute to organ damage.
choices.note: Correct. Those three statements are the whole of the second septic-shock page.

choices.text: The researchers named on the page blame clots in large veins only.
choices.note: The page says some researchers think blood clots in small arteries cause the lack of blood flow.

choices.text: The inflammatory response protects organs from the toxins.
choices.note: The page says the strong inflammatory response may contribute to organ damage.

scene: The doctor writes a septic workup and the student reads the blood-test examples.
ask: What blood tests are named, and what is CBP for?

choices.text: CBP is the urine culture, and blood culture is not listed.
choices.note: CBP is complete blood picture; urine culture on this page is MSU x C/ST or CSU x C/ST.

choices.text: The only blood test named is a chest X-ray.
choices.note: CXR is on the next workup page, not in this blood-test list.

choices.text: L/RFT means the sputum culture.
choices.note: Sputum culture is Spt x C/ST; L/RFT is liver and renal function.

choices.text: Bld x C/ST for blood culture, CBP as complete blood picture to observe any white-cell increase, and L/RFT for liver and renal function.
choices.note: Correct. The page gives those three blood examples and glosses CBP as complete blood picture to observe any white blood cell increase, and L/RFT as liver and renal function.

scene: The same workup also asks about urine and sputum.
ask: Which specimens does the note name?

choices.text: A urine stick for glucose and protein only, with no culture.
choices.note: Glucose and protein by urine stick are on a perioperative page; this page names MSU or CSU culture.

choices.text: Catheter urine only, never a mid-stream specimen.
choices.note: Both MSU x C/ST and CSU x C/ST are listed.

choices.text: MSU x C/ST or CSU x C/ST, asked as a check for urinary tract infection, and Spt x C/ST for sputum.
choices.note: Correct. The page lists mid-stream urine culture or catheterized urine culture, and sputum culture.

choices.text: Sputum culture written as Bld x C/ST.
choices.note: Bld x C/ST is the blood culture; sputum is Spt x C/ST.

scene: The workup continues on the next page, beyond the cultures already named.
ask: What imaging example is printed there?

choices.text: CXR, a chest X-ray.
choices.note: Correct. The second workup page starts with CXR (Chest X-ray).

choices.text: An ankle X-ray as the named film.
choices.note: The page names a chest X-ray, not an ankle film.

choices.text: A 12-lead ECG as the workup imaging.
choices.note: A 12-lead ECG is in the low blood-pressure remarks, not this workup list.

choices.text: Wound-bed slough grading instead of a film.
choices.note: Wound-bed words are in the later wound-care page, not this workup line.

scene: The patient is still febrile and someone reaches for Panadol before the antibiotic review.
ask: What does this workup page say about Panadol?

choices.text: Intravenous Panadol 1 g is required so the fever chart stays flat.
choices.note: The page says +/- oral or per rectal Panadol, and it does not print a 1 g intravenous dose.

choices.text: Panadol must be given or the blood cultures cannot be taken.
choices.note: The page does not tie cultures to a compulsory Panadol dose; it allows Panadol to be left unprescribed.

choices.text: Panadol is withheld only when the temperature is already normal.
choices.note: The reason printed is observing the fever pattern to check antibiotics, not a normal temperature.

choices.text: Panadol is marked +/- and may be oral or per rectal. If the doctor wants to watch the fever pattern to check the effect of antibiotics, he may not prescribe Panadol.
choices.note: Correct. That is the parenthetical remark on the page: he may not prescribe Panadol to a fever patient when observing the fever pattern against antibiotics.

scene: Intravenous antibiotics are added and the student reads the examples on the page.
ask: Which antibiotic examples are actually printed?

choices.text: Augmentin 1.2g Q6H and Tazocin 4.5g once a day.
choices.note: Both Augmentin and Tazocin are printed as Q8H, not Q6H or once daily.

choices.text: Augmentin 1.2g Q8H, Tazocin 4.5g Q8H, and Meropenem with no dose written beside the name.
choices.note: Correct. The page says +/- intravenous antibiotics, e.g. Augmentin 1.2g Q8H, Tazocin 4.5g Q8H, Meropenem.

choices.text: Meropenem 1g Q8H as a dose this page states.
choices.note: Meropenem is named, but no dose is printed beside it.

choices.text: No intravenous antibiotic example, only oral Panadol.
choices.note: The page includes the intravenous antibiotic examples as well as +/- Panadol.

scene: The cuff looks narrow on the arm and the systolic reading jumps.
ask: What result and reason does the cuff page give for a cuff that is too narrow?

choices.text: Systolic blood pressure increases 10 to 40 mmHg, because it takes extra pressure to compress the brachial artery.
choices.note: Correct. That is the narrow-cuff row: measurement increase 10 to 40 mmHg, extra pressure to compress the brachial artery.

choices.text: Systolic pressure falls 10 to 40 mmHg because the artery is compressed too easily.
choices.note: Cutting off the artery too easily is the rationale for a falsely low reading from a loose or ballooning cuff, not the narrow-cuff row.

choices.text: Systolic pressure increases 10 to 50 mmHg from the narrow cuff.
choices.note: 10 to 50 mmHg is the clothing row, not the narrow-cuff row.

choices.text: The reading does not change if the cuff is only a little narrow.
choices.note: The page states an increase of 10 to 40 mmHg for a cuff too narrow for the extremity.

scene: The cuff is too loose, the wrap is uneven, and the bladder balloons out.
ask: What reading does the note expect, and why?

choices.text: A systolic rise of 10 to 40 mmHg, as with a narrow cuff.
choices.note: The 10 to 40 mmHg rise is the narrow-cuff result, not the loose-cuff result.

choices.text: A systolic rise of 10 to 50 mmHg, as with clothing.
choices.note: Clothing is the 10 to 50 mmHg row.

choices.text: A falsely low blood pressure, because the cuff cuts off the brachial artery supply too easily and the monitor gives a lower reading than it should.
choices.note: Correct. That is the loose, uneven, or ballooning-bladder row and its rationale.

choices.text: No error, because a loose cuff is the recommended fit.
choices.note: The page lists this fit as a common problem with a falsely low result.

scene: The student leaves a thick sleeve under the cuff.
ask: What can clothing do to the systolic reading?

choices.text: It always lowers systolic pressure by 10 mmHg.
choices.note: The page says clothing can increase the systolic reading, not lower it by a fixed 10 mmHg.

choices.text: Depending on the thickness of the fabric, clothing can increase systolic blood pressure from 10 to 50 mmHg.
choices.note: Correct. The clothing row says clothing can increase a systolic blood pressure from 10 to 50 mmHg, depending on fabric thickness.

choices.text: It has no effect once the cuff size is correct.
choices.note: Cuff over clothing is still listed as its own common problem.

choices.text: It raises every systolic reading by exactly 40 mmHg.
choices.note: A 10 to 40 mmHg rise is the narrow-cuff figure; clothing is 10 to 50 mmHg and depends on thickness.

scene: The patient is lying on one side and the cuffed arm is above heart level.
ask: What does this page say that position does?

choices.text: It gives a falsely high blood pressure because the arm is above the heart.
choices.note: The page says above heart level provides a falsely low BP, not a high one.

choices.text: Side-lying always matches a sitting reading.
choices.note: The rationale is that readings vary depending on distance from the heart.

choices.text: It is the position you should use to confirm a low reading before charting.
choices.note: It is listed as a common problem, not as the charting method.

choices.text: Above heart level it provides a falsely low blood pressure, and readings vary with distance from the heart.
choices.note: Correct. The side-lying row says above heart level provides a falsely low BP, with varied readings depending on distance from the heart.

scene: The first systolic reading is above 160 mmHg.
ask: What does the high blood-pressure action start with?

choices.text: Put the feet higher than the head by 15-30 degrees.
choices.note: Feet higher than the head is a later step on the low blood-pressure page, not this high reading.

choices.text: Report to the doctor before any cuff or talking check.
choices.note: The numbered actions start with clothing, cuff size, stop talking, and a bilateral recheck, and the report goes to the team nurse.

choices.text: Make sure there is no clothing blockage, use the correct cuff size, stop talking, and recheck both limbs.
choices.note: Correct. For SBP > 160 mmHg the first action is no clothing blockage, correct cuff size, stop talking, and recheck bilateral limb.

choices.text: Use this same first step for any systolic reading above 140 mmHg.
choices.note: The threshold printed on this page is SBP > 160 mmHg.

scene: The pressure is still high after that recheck. The patient has no headache.
ask: What does the page say about the next measure, the report, and the repeat check?

choices.text: Invite the patient back to bed and keep them relaxed, report to the team nurse after the blood-pressure routine, and recheck blood pressure and pulse after 15-30 minutes.
choices.note: Correct. Actions 2 to 4 say return to bed and keep relax, report after the routine unless there is headache, and recheck BP/P after 15-30 minutes.

choices.text: Report every high reading immediately, headache or not.
choices.note: Immediate report on this page is if the patient suffers with headache; otherwise after the routine.

choices.text: Recheck only the pulse after 2 hours.
choices.note: The page says recheck patient BP/P after 15-30 minutes.

choices.text: Have the patient exercise before the next reading.
choices.note: The nursing care says stop exercise and talking, and rest on the bed.

scene: You are settling the patient after the high reading and the team nurse explains the follow-up.
ask: What nursing care and remarks are printed?

choices.text: Walk the patient and take the call bell away.
choices.note: Care says rest on bed, give a call bell, stop exercise and talking, and put on the bedside rail.

choices.text: Stop all blood-pressure checks until the next day.
choices.note: The remark says the team nurse will increase monitoring to Q4H or Q1H.

choices.text: Start an inotrope before any ECG.
choices.note: Inotrope is on the low blood-pressure remarks; this page says antihypertensive agents after investigation such as ECG or blood test.

choices.text: Rest on the bed, give the call bell, stop exercise and talking, and put the bedside rail up. Monitoring may increase to Q4H or Q1H. The doctor may order antihypertensive agents after investigation such as ECG or a blood test.
choices.note: Correct. That is the nursing-care box and the remarks on the high blood-pressure page.

scene: Systolic pressure stays under 90 mmHg after you have checked the cuff and brought the patient back to bed.
ask: What position does this page then tell you to try for the measurement?

choices.text: Head higher than the feet by 15-30 degrees.
choices.note: The page says feet higher than the head, not the head higher than the feet.

choices.text: Feet higher than the head by 15-30 degrees.
choices.note: Correct. If the record is still low after return to bed, attempt to measure BP with the feet higher than the head by 15-30 degrees. Earlier you must already have checked there is no limb elevation or clothing blockage and that the cuff size is correct, and rechecked both limbs.

choices.text: Leave the limbs up from the start, because elevation is the first instruction.
choices.note: Action 1 says make sure there is no elevation of limbs; the feet-higher position is a later attempt if the bed reading is still low.

scene: During observations the pulse oximeter reads under 90%.

choices.note: Correct. The page says make sure SpO2 is not affected by cold or circulation, recheck bilateral limbs, and chart the highest one.

scene: You hear a sputum sound while the saturation is being checked.

scene: The patient has COPD and you are setting the saturation target before giving oxygen.

choices.note: The page says high CO2 concentration in blood will increase the RR in normal people.

choices.note: Correct. The page says COPD patients experience a chronic condition of high CO2 level in blood, and the brain CO2 sensor is deactivated.

choices.note: Correct. That is the page: O2 level is the only mechanism, high O2 lets RR be reduced, decreased RR worsens CO2 retention, and that Cantonese warning is printed.

scene: The routine meter reads under 4 mmol/L. You need to know who to tell, and how fast.
